title: POC weekly latency tuning - Rivermark
next_steps: Diego to run TTFT+streaming burst test and share results
Avery to send updated pricing for dedicated vs hosted latency SLOs
Customer to share representative prompt set and p95/p99 targets
Schedule follow-up on 2027-06-30 to review benchmarks
action_items: Diego Ruiz: Run TTFT benchmark with seq_len=512, streaming on, quantized kernels where possible (due: 2027-06-28)
Rana Mohan: Export current API tail latency (p95/p99) and sample traces (due: 2027-06-26)
Avery Chen: Send Redwood kernel selector matrix and updated pricing for dedicated pools (due: 2027-06-27)
Lena Brooks: Share 200 representative prompts and typical session lengths (due: 2027-06-25)
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on reducing time-to-first-token (TTFT) and end-to-end latency. Reviewed last week's benchmark (TTFT ~210ms on hosted with no streaming), discussed enabling streaming and kernel selection to lower TTFT and tail latency. Decided to run targeted TTFT burst tests with streaming and seq_len=512, share prompt set, and have Redwood send kernel selector matrix and pricing options for dedicated capacity.
transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. quick hour, we'll go through the benchmark updates, tuning notes, and action items. Sam, Rana, Lena, Ivy, you all good?
[00:08] Sam Patel: Yep, all good. can hear you.
[00:10] Rana Mohan: Good here.
[00:12] Lena Brooks: good
[00:15] Avery Chen: Awesome. Diego and Maya from Redwood are on, Diego is gonna cover the kernel and batching stuff.
[00:20] Diego Ruiz: Hey team. quick recap: last week we ran your baseline against our hosted endpoint using model-redwood-v1 (roughly a trimmed 7b variant). TTFT averaged ~210 ms, p95 ~420 ms, p99 ~880 ms, that was without streaming and with default kernel selection.
[00:40] Ivy Park: just to clarify — that's for the 256 token prompts right?
[00:45] Diego Ruiz: yeah most tests were seq_len=256, typical session length 2-3 exchanges. Some longer prompts hit 512 and we saw TTFT creep up to ~350ms.
[01:00] Sam Patel: Our SLA goal for customer-facing flows is p95 < 300ms, ideally <200ms TTFT. So need to push down.
[01:10] Avery Chen: Got it. so two levers: enable streaming to reduce perceived TTFT and tweak kernel choices/quantization plus batching to reduce actual token latencies.
[01:22] Diego Ruiz: Correct. Also prefix/KV cache can help for multi-turns — note your workload is a lot of repeated system prompt tokens so cache should help a lot.
[01:35] Rana Mohan: we've got sessions with identical context across calls, so KV cache sounds promising, but how does that effect cold-start TTFT?
[01:45] Diego Ruiz: cold-start TTFT won't benefit from KV cache; cache helps after the first token. For cold starts we want optimized kernels and streaming to push the first token faster.
[01:55] Maya Singh: one other tradeoff, quantized kernels (8-bit/4-bit) lower memory and can reduce throughput latency in some cases but can increase compute for first token due to dequantization overhead on certain GPUs, depends on kernel selection.
[02:12] Lena Brooks: that's the thing — we're on provisioned GPU pools for other workloads but for this POC we're hitting hosted. if we move to dedicated, would those kernels behave differently?
[02:25] Diego Ruiz: yes, on Dedicated (customer pools) we can pin to specific kernel implementations and use GPU arch-specific kernels (A100 vs H100 optimizations) which gives better TTFT and lower tail. With Redwood Dedicated you also get predictable warm-up state.
[02:40] Sam Patel: can you quantify? like how much TTFT improvement if we go Dedicated and enable streaming?
[02:46] Diego Ruiz: ballpark — on H100 optimized kernels we often see TTFT drop from 200–300ms range to ~120–160ms for the same model with streaming and warm workers. P95 down to ~220–300ms. but depends on seq_len and batching profile.
[03:00] Ivy Park: Our concerns: security/auditing, and also cost — dedicated sounds pricey.
[03:07] Avery Chen: understood. we'll send pricing options comparing hosted vs dedicated with throughput tiers. Avery: action item.
[03:14] Sam Patel: also curious about streaming vs non-streaming — for us streaming is acceptable but we need final answer tokens to come in consistent order and not partial hallucinations.
[03:24] Maya Singh: streaming just affects delivery, not model output ordering; you should see chunks of tokens as generated. the only time we see partial is if client drops connection. We also have an option for chunked streaming that waits until a punctuation boundary for consumer-friendly rendering.
[03:40] Rana Mohan: Diego, earlier you mentioned kernel selector heuristics — can you walk through that?
[03:46] Diego Ruiz: sure — our runtime chooses kernels based on model dims, token length distribution, and hardware. e.g., for causual attention with short sequences we pick a kernel optimized for low-latency single-token generation; for long sequences we switch to tiled kernels that are throughput-optimized. there's a heuristic threshold at around seq_len ~384 where we may switch. you can override with a profile for the Dedicated runs.
[04:10] Sam Patel: so if most of our sessions are 512, should we force the long-seq kernels?
[04:15] Diego Ruiz: yes, forcing long-seq kernels can help throughput, but TTFT might increase a bit for the very first token due to larger kernel init; again streaming reduces perceived TTFT.
[04:28] Ivy Park: what about batching? are you batching across users? that increases latency.
[04:33] Diego Ruiz: we use dynamic continuous batching: we batch but cap wait at low ms limits depending on the SLO. for low-latency routes we set max wait 5-10ms and prioritise single-token fast path; for bulk routes we allow higher wait to improve throughput.
[04:50] Lena Brooks: can we see the config you used for the last run? like batch windows, kernel choices?
[04:55] Diego Ruiz: yes — we'll share the runbook and kernel selector matrix. Avery will attach after.
[05:02] Avery Chen: I'll send the matrix and our suggested config for seq_len 256 and 512.
[05:07] Sam Patel: great. any quick wins we can do before another run?
[05:10] Maya Singh: enable streaming + reduce initial context size where possible; trim system prompt, use KV cache for repeated contexts, set max batch wait to 5ms for the low-latency route. That combo usually drops TTFT ~40–60ms.
[05:24] Rana Mohan: we can try trimming. one question on metrics: how are you measuring TTFT — from client perspective or server-side?
[05:31] Diego Ruiz: both. our measurement: server-side time from request arrival to first token emitted; client-side includes network. We'll provide both metrics in the report.
[05:40] Ivy Park: network is a variable here; some customers are mobile heavy so client delta is big.
[05:45] Diego Ruiz: yep, consider edge routing or regional endpoints if network is large factor.
[05:52] Sam Patel: earlier you mentioned p99 was quite high (~880ms). what's the typical root cause?
[05:58] Diego Ruiz: tail often caused by occasional long sequences, cold workers, or queuing spikes during batching. On hosted, noisy neighbors can also cause spikes; Dedicated mitigates that. Also kernel fallbacks when memory pressure occurs can spike latencies.
[06:12] Lena Brooks: can we set an auto-fallback to a smaller model if tail triggers?
[06:18] Diego Ruiz: yes — Redwood runtime supports policy-based fallbacks: if queued time crosses threshold we can route to a smaller-compatible model variant. We'll help set that policy.
[06:28] Avery Chen: that's often a good engineering compromise — keep UX consistent while protecting SLOs.
[06:34] Ivy Park: ok, for today's run — what's the plan and what do you need from us?
[06:38] Diego Ruiz: Plan: 1) Diego runs TTFT+streaming burst test with seq_len=256 and 512; 2) use streaming and non-streaming toggles; 3) test with default kernel selection and forced long-seq kernel; 4) collect server-side TTFT, p95/p99 client emulated numbers. We need: prompt set and target p95.
[06:57] Sam Patel: target p95 <300ms, TTFT ideally <150ms but 200ms acceptable.
[07:05] Avery Chen: noted. Diego you'll run tests this week and share csvs, Maya will help interpret.
[07:12] Diego Ruiz: yes. I plan to run tests tonight and post results in the shared sheet. results will include per-route config: batch wait, kernel config, streaming on/off, seq_len, TTFT, p95, p99, throughput.
[07:25] Lena Brooks: any risk with enabling streaming for our customers from a compliance perspective?
[07:30] Avery Chen: streaming doesn't change data residency or logs; it's just chunked responses. We can ensure same audit logs are emitted. If you need additional encryption-in-transit options we can walk through.
[07:41] Sam Patel: we also want to know how this maps to cost. streaming might add overhead on the server side?
[07:46] Diego Ruiz: streaming has marginal compute overhead; cost impact is small, but if you reduce latency and increase throughput you may actually save. Dedicated pricing will be more predictable; we'll include estimates.
[07:58] Ivy Park: any items on kernel quantization? do you recommend 4-bit?
[08:03] Maya Singh: 4-bit can be great for throughput but for latency-sensitive paths we recommend model-level testing. sometimes 8-bit gives best TTFT on certain GPU archs because dequantization cost is lower. We'll test both in the benchmark.
[08:18] Sam Patel: sounds good. can we also get a trace of a slow request? p99 case?
[08:23] Diego Ruiz: yes — Rana, if you can share a few sample traces or logs we'll correlate with our server traces.
[08:30] Rana Mohan: will do. I'll export logs and share in the sheet.
[08:34] Avery Chen: perfect. anything else on the tuning side?
[08:38] Maya Singh: just one more note — if you enable KV cache, make sure to set the right cache eviction and key sizing; we can propose defaults. poor cache sizing can make things worse.
[08:49] Lena Brooks: can you share cache defaults?
[08:51] Diego Ruiz: yes, will include in the runbook.
[08:55] Ivy Park: timeline — when can we reconvene to review results?
[08:58] Avery Chen: propose 2027-06-30, same time. does that work?
[09:03] Sam Patel: works for us.
[09:05] Rana Mohan: works.
[09:07] Avery Chen: ok next steps recap: Diego run tests, Maya interpret, Avery send pricing + kernel matrix, Rivermark share prompts + traces. We'll meet 6/30 to review.
[09:19] Ivy Park: quick note — we might involve procurement if dedicated looks like the path.
[09:24] Avery Chen: acknowledged. we'll prep a short procurement checklist.
[09:27] Diego Ruiz: One final technical Q from me — are you seeing a lot of variable sequence length across sessions or pretty uniform?
[09:34] Sam Patel: variable; most are short but ~15% go to 512.
[09:39] Diego Ruiz: okay that explains some of the tail. we'll include mixed seq_len runs.
[09:45] Lena Brooks: thanks everyone.
[09:46] Avery Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[09:49] [meeting ends]
